claims.claim: The rollout decision that impersonation goes behind a per-project flag cannot be executed against the design as specified: RFC-001 states as a goal that the feature can be enabled or disabled only at the system level and that once set it applies to all Argo CD Applications, with the switch being application.sync.impersonation.enabled in argocd-cm, the ARGOCD_APPLICATION_CONTROLLER_ENABLE_IMPERSONATION environment variable, or the --enable-impersonation flag, none of which are per-project. Operationally there is no knob to turn on for one project, so the first project that opts in changes the sync identity for every Application on the instance.

The CI diff failures in T-26271 are the instance-wide blast radius of that same system-level switch: the reporter says the failing jobs are all in projects where the sync impersonation flag was recently enabled and cannot explain why the diff runs with a narrower identity than the broad cluster Secret credential, and the platform sync call root-caused it as diff running as the destination service account, which does not hold patch on cluster-scoped resources. The detection path is a fatal CI job failure with an RBAC message naming system:serviceaccount:argocd:argocd-server, and the root cause exists only in a call note, so the on-call reader of the ticket has no runbook linking the error to the flag they flipped.

T-28695 is the diff path that RFC-001's implementation list never enumerated: RFC-001 assigns the GitOps Engine component the task of honoring the Impersonate configuration for the kubectl commands executed during sync, and fixes sync.go to set Impersonate on the SyncContext, but names no component for the comparison path. So Server-Side Diff continues to run as the cluster Secret credential rather than the AppProject's destinationServiceAccounts, and on external clusters the App rotates Synced and Unknown on every reconcile with a ComparisonError as the only signal.

The stated gate that nobody flips impersonation on a project until the diff story is fixed leaves the standing workaround as the operating procedure: ServerSideDiff=false set per Application on every external-cluster Application, forever, plus a ratchet of patch rules on the cluster role for each new resource kind a chart introduces, already five rounds with no end state. That is unbudgeted recurring toil with no owner named, and because Kubernetes RBAC has no dry-run verb, every grant added to unblock a diff is real write authority on a deliberately least-privilege identity.

The roadmap and the PRD state opposite commitments about ApplicationSet teardown: the roadmap says deletion of generated Applications is explicitly out of scope for rollout orchestration, that ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented, and that teardown remains a manual operator action performed one Application at a time, while the PRD introduces the deletionOrder field on ApplicationSetStrategy with AllAtOnce and Reverse values that do exactly that ordering. Whichever an operator reads becomes their teardown procedure, and no owner is assigned to reconcile the two.

The teardown procedure the roadmap documents is the precise action that reproduces the delete and recreate loop: the roadmap tells operators to tear down ApplicationSet children manually, one Application at a time, and T-28511 reproduces an infinite Deleting-to-Syncing flip when a generated Application under Progressive Sync is deleted manually outside the controller's purview while a deployed resource holds it in Progressing. Following the documented manual teardown on a Progressive Sync ApplicationSet is therefore the trigger, and the operator's only signal is watching the status flip in the UI.

The PRD records No immediate Risks to consider and confines its Upgrade and Downgrade Strategy to CRD field addition, but T-28511 shows the Reverse semantics the PRD specifies, waiting for one Application to be fully deleted before moving onto the next, deadlocks when the resource holding an Application in Progressing never finishes deleting, and the controller restarts the wave from the top. Deletion is past the point of no return: there is no rollback for a Reverse teardown that stalls mid-sequence, since the Applications already deleted are gone and the CRD downgrade path the PRD describes does not restore them.

The incident review's standing rule, switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before deleting any child app by hand, is a runbook line with nothing enforcing it. The only validation the PRD specifies is a check correlating the deletion strategy to the ApplicationSet strategy, namely that Reverse may only be selected when rollingSync lists an order, which passes cleanly on exactly the configuration that triggers the loop. deletionOrder stays a freely editable spec field, so an operator who has not read the review note is not stopped and no alert fires.

The team deprioritized the one mechanism that would give the deletion work a revert path and moved the same dev pair onto the deletion loop: T-27327 is what makes rollback with the source hydrator work, checking out the old rendered manifests and pushing them to the sync branch, and until it lands the History and Rollback tab has no rollback for hydrator-backed Applications. So a progressive sync deletion that fails mid-way on a hydrated repo leaves the operator running that git checkout and push sequence by hand at whatever hour it breaks.

T-27949's failure mode is undetectable with what exists today: the rollout reports complete while the child Applications are OutOfSync because status.applicationStatus stays Healthy and syncDesiredApplications only syncs Applications in Pending, and the reporter notes the ApplicationSet controller logs were at warn level so no progressive-sync transition logs were emitted. The metrics that would answer my sync is not starting, why or which Applications is it waiting for are still only a proposal in T-27846, so nothing pages anyone and the discovery path is a human or a customer noticing the drift.

The restriction that hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until there is a debounce exists only as an interim call in the incident review, and the review itself records that the pilot ticket should carry it so the next team does not trip it. T-27949 is a live report from precisely that configuration, a pilot repo where every hydration cycle lands a fresh commit on the hydrated branch and each is picked up as a source change. Nothing in the ticket or the controller carries the restriction forward, so the next team onboarding the hydrator inherits the wave-restart loop with no warning.

Enabling commitserver.sign.hydrated.commits turns a key problem into a fleet-wide hydration stop: T-28239 specifies fail fast with no silent fallback, the commit server failing at startup if the key is missing or invalid, and RFC-002 routes every hydrated push through that single commit server via the CommitManifests call. The visible symptom is the absence of new commits on the hydrated branch, so Applications keep syncing the last hydrated manifests and stay Synced and Healthy while their dry source moves on. Nothing in either document names a signal for a hydrator that has stopped producing.

The hydrator's recurring credential burden is two secrets plus a policy that must move together: RFC-002 requires a repository-write Secret holding the githubAppPrivateKey for push access, and T-28239 adds a mounted GPG signing key Secret whose public half must be registered in argocd-gpg-keys-cm and in the project's SourceIntegrity policy. Rotating the signing key without updating both of those reproduces the exact condition T-28239 was filed to remove, Argo CD rejecting its own hydrated output, and nobody budgets that rotation because it is not a feature.

The external system that RFC-002's push-to-stage mode relies on to move changes from the staging branch to the deployment branch is the stage-branch promoter that the platform sync call identified as still a shell script with nobody owning it, and that item was parked rather than assigned. Push-to-stage therefore has a deployment gate with no on-call owner: when promotion stalls, the deployed state simply stops advancing and there is no one whose rotation covers it.

When that unowned promoter is slow or stopped, T-26443 is the resulting deploy: it is observed only in push-to-stage mode, where the external promoter has not yet moved the fresh manifests, so auto-sync picks up whatever the stage branch last held and immediately syncs stale manifests. There is no freshness check today, the proposed annotation-based block is still a proposal, and the failure is silent because the Application reports Synced against old content, so detection is someone noticing the workload is on an old revision.

Parallel progressive sync steps remove the rate limiter nobody accounted for: T-28755 replaces the sequential barrier, where step N+1 cannot begin until every application matched by step N is healthy, with parallel groups spanning staging and production clusters at once, while T-29001 records that QPS and Burst are still global via ARGOCD_K8S_CLIENT_QPS and ARGOCD_K8S_CLIENT_BURST for all managed destination clusters. Fanning out concurrent syncs under one global budget lands on the lowest common denominator problem T-29001 describes, with under-provisioned edge clusters hitting API server throttling, elevated latencies, or API server crashes at the moment a release is going out.

T-28927 scopes promotion of Progressive Sync to Stable around key execution issues being addressed and names the out-of-order sync blocker resolved for v3.6, while T-28927's own definition of Stable is that issues will thereafter be tracked as bugs with fixes shipped as patches. T-27949 is an open v3.4.2 defect in which the rollout reports complete with children OutOfSync, which is a silent-success failure rather than an execution failure, so the maturity bar as written can be met while the mode that produces undetected drift remains open and support inherits it under a stability promise.

The mitigation T-27833 proposes, splitting which resources the Argo CD control plane handles from which the impersonated service account handles so the impersonated identity can be stripped of Namespace permissions, is incompatible with RFC-001 as designed: RFC-001 states the service account for impersonation is determined on a per Application level rather than on per resource level, with Application.spec.destination.namespace choosing one account for all resources in the Application. Until that changes, review-environment ApplicationSets have no boundary preventing a committed Namespace resource from overwriting the managedNamespaceMetadata labels, including pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce, and the AppProject RBAC deny policy does not fire because it governs API and UI actions, not the controller's apply.
